jdso8u-d1e110-d1e107.summary: Editorial title of the third prologue question (Wadding numbering): whether theology is about God as its first subject.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e132.summary: Announces that the negative will be argued in two ways, the first being to show the negative directly.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e146.summary: First argument for the negative, from Boethius (De Trinitate I): a simple form cannot be a subject; God is a simple form, so cannot be the subject of a science.
claims: A simple form cannot be a subject (Boethius).

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e162.summary: Second argument: the material cause does not coincide with the other causes, neither numerically nor specifically (Physics II). God is the final and efficient cause of this science, so he cannot be its matter, i.e. its subject.
claims: Material cause does not coincide with efficient or final cause.
God is the efficient and final cause of theology, so not its subject.
concepts: God as end and agent of theology

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e183.summary: Third argument, from Posterior Analytics I: the subject of a science has parts, principles and attributes. God has no integral parts (being simple), no subjective parts (being singular of himself), no principles (being the first principle), and no attributes, since an attribute inheres in a subject outside its essence and nothing so inheres in God.
claims: The subject of a science has parts, principles and attributes.
God has none of these.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e212.summary: Second way of arguing the negative: something else is the subject. Augustine (De doctrina christiana I) says every teaching concerns things or signs, so things or signs are the subject. Also, Scripture has four senses (anagogical, tropological, allegorical, literal), and each sense would correspond to its own first subject, so there are four subjects.
claims: All teaching concerns things or signs (Augustine).
Each scriptural sense would have its own subject.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e267.summary: Third argument that man is the subject, from Averroes on Ethics I: moral science is about man as to soul, medicine about man as to body. Hence every practical science has as first subject that for which its end is acquired, not the end itself; theology's end is acquired for man, not God.
claims: A practical science's subject is that for which its end is acquired.
Theology's end is acquired for man, so man is its subject.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e304.summary: A variant: a science's end is to reach its first object by its act, inducing in it the form principally intended (being known, for speculative science; the form its praxis aims at, for practical science). Theology intends moral goodness, which is induced in man, not God, so man is its first object.
claims: A science's end is to induce its intended form in its first object.
Theology intends moral goodness, which is induced in man.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e339.summary: Argument for the affirmative from Augustine (City of God VIII.1): theology is discourse or reasoning about God.
claims: Theology is discourse about God (Augustine).

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e356.summary: Editorial title of the first 'lateral' (subsidiary) question: whether theology is about God under some special ratio.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e369.summary: Argument for the affirmative from Hugh of St Victor (De sacramentis): the works of restoration are the subject; so if God is the subject, it is under a special ratio, as restorer.
claims: The works of restoration are theology's subject (Hugh of St Victor).
So God would be subject as restorer.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e401.summary: Argument from Cassiodorus on the Psalms: Christ, head with members, is the subject; so God would be subject specifically as incarnate and head of the Church.
claims: The whole Christ, head and members, is theology's subject (Cassiodorus).

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e420.summary: Argument: God absolutely is the subject of metaphysics, so if he is theology's subject it must be under some special ratio, since he is not subject in both under exactly the same ratio. Proof: Aristotle (Metaphysics VI) says the most honorable science is about the noblest genus, and he calls metaphysics theology.
claims: God absolutely is the subject of metaphysics.
So theology must treat God under a special ratio.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e459.summary: Support: Averroes (Physics I, last comment) says Avicenna erred in having metaphysics prove the first cause exists, since the genus of separate substances is its subject and no science proves its own subject exists. The argument works only if God is its first subject.
claims: No science proves the existence of its subject.
Averroes takes separate substances, and so God, as metaphysics' subject.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e491.summary: Argument: this science is most honorable, so its subject is most honorable under the most honorable ratio, which is the ratio of end and good. Avicenna says the science of the end would be noblest among sciences of causes; and since denying ends destroys the good (Metaphysics II), the ratio of good is that of end.
claims: The most honorable science treats its subject under the most honorable ratio.
The ratio of end and good is the most honorable.
So theology treats God as end and good.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e539.summary: Argument against the lateral question: contracted knowledge presupposes absolute knowledge, which is more certain (Metaphysics I). If theology were about God under a special ratio, there would be a prior and more certain knowledge of God absolutely, which is not posited.
claims: Knowledge under a special ratio presupposes more certain absolute knowledge.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e562.summary: Editorial title of the second lateral question: whether this science concerns all things by their attribution to its first subject.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e578.summary: Argument for the affirmative from Metaphysics IV: one science treats something and what is attributed to it (as with 'healthy'); everything else is essentially attributed to theology's first subject.
claims: One science treats a thing and what is attributed to it.
All things are attributed to theology's first subject.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e603.summary: Argument against, from Augustine (De Trinitate XIV.1), who denies that everything knowable is to be attributed to this science.
claims: Not everything knowable belongs to theology (Augustine).

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e618.summary: Scotus sets out his procedure for solving the three questions: first distinguish theology in itself from theology in us; second, determine the notion of first subject; third, distinguish the parts of theology.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e640.summary: First distinction: knowledge in itself is what the object is apt to produce of itself in an intellect proportioned to it; knowledge in us is what our intellect is apt to have of that object. Theology in itself is the knowledge the theological object would produce in a proportioned intellect; theology in us is what our intellect can have of it. Example: for someone unable to understand geometry but able to believe a geometer, geometry would be faith for him, but still science in itself.
claims: Knowledge in itself is defined by what the object can cause in a proportioned intellect.
Knowledge in us is defined by what our intellect can have.
A science in itself can be faith for a given knower.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e697.summary: Second: the ratio of first subject is to contain first and virtually all truths of the habit. Proof: the first object contains the immediate propositions, since their subject contains the predicate and so the evidence of the whole proposition; immediate propositions contain the conclusions; so the subject of immediate propositions contains all truths of the habit.
claims: The first subject of a science virtually contains first all the truths of that science.
The subject contains the evidence of immediate propositions, which contain the conclusions.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e739.summary: Second proof: 'first' here is taken from the definition of the universal in Posterior Analytics I as signifying adequacy. The object relates to the habit as cause to effect, and a cause is adequate only if it contains first and virtually the whole effect.
claims: 'First' signifies adequacy.
An adequate cause contains first and virtually its whole effect.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e764.summary: Explanation of 'first virtually': as the first being depends on nothing else while others depend on it, so to contain first is not to depend on others in containing, while others depend on it; that is, even if, per impossibile, everything else were removed, with its concept remaining, it would still contain the truths, and nothing else contains them except through its ratio.
claims: To contain first means to contain independently, while others contain only through it.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e792.summary: First objection to this account: the first object of a habit stands to the habit as a power's first object to the power; but a power's first object is something common to all its per se objects; so a habit's first object is something common, not something virtually containing the others.
claims: A power's first object is common to all its per se objects.
By parity, a habit's first object should be common rather than virtually containing.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e823.summary: Second objection: in the sciences the first subject commonly assigned is something common to everything the science considers: line in geometry, number in arithmetic, being in metaphysics.
claims: Sciences usually take as subject something common to all they consider.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e845.summary: Reply to the first objection: object to power is the relation of mover to movable, active to passive; subject to habit is cause to effect. In the active-passive relation, any agent of a kind can act on any patient of the corresponding kind, so the first terms are the most common and adequate to each other. In the cause-effect relation the first terms are not the most common, since a common item's causing the habit does not mean a special one can, and conversely; not everything under the common regards the habit as its effect, only a first containing object that virtually contains all the habit extends to.
claims: Object-power is an active-passive relation whose first terms are the most common.
Subject-habit is a cause-effect relation whose first term is a virtually containing object, not the most common one.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e915.summary: Reply to the second objection: many specifically distinct habits can have a common object abstracted from their objects, and this is how sciences are assigned common objects; but then the habit is one only in genus, not in species.
claims: A common subject abstracted from several objects unifies habits only generically.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e942.summary: Third: theology essentially contains contingent truths as well as necessary ones. Truths about God as triune or about a divine person in relation ad intra are necessary (that God is triune, that the Son is begotten). Those relating God ad extra are contingent (that God was, that the Son became incarnate). All truths about God as triune or about a determinate person are theological, as are the contingent ones, since they belong to no natural knowledge. So theology's first integral parts are necessary and contingent truths.
claims: Truths about God ad intra are necessary; truths about God ad extra are contingent.
Both kinds are theological, since neither falls under natural knowledge.
Theology's two first integral parts are necessary and contingent truths.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1003.summary: Answer to the first question regarding theology in itself as to its necessary truths: its first subject can only be God. First of three reasons: the first object virtually contains all the habit's truths, and only God virtually contains all theological truths, since nothing else contains them as cause or as that to which they are attributed (God being attributed to nothing), nor as an effect via demonstration quia, since no effect demonstrates God as triune, the chief theological truth.
claims: The first subject of theology in itself is God.
Only God virtually contains all theological truths.
No effect demonstrates the Trinity.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1061.summary: Second reason: theology concerns what is naturally known only to the divine intellect, so it concerns something naturally known to God alone, and only God is naturally known to himself alone. The antecedent: if theology were about things naturally known to another intellect, the infinite divine intellect would know more, so there would be a higher science; the minor: every created essence can be naturally known by some created intellect (e.g. an angel).
claims: Theology concerns what is naturally known only to the divine intellect.
Every created essence is naturally knowable to some created intellect.
Only God is naturally known to God alone.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1111.summary: Third reason: no science gives as distinct knowledge of something not its first subject as a science of which it is the first subject would; otherwise there would be no reason why that subject is more its subject than another. If God were not theology's subject, theology would not give as distinct knowledge of God as a science with God as subject could; but such a science is possible, and it would be prior to this one.
claims: A science gives the most distinct knowledge of its own first subject.
If God were not theology's subject, a science about God would be prior to theology.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1157.summary: Beyond the three reasons, some persuasive arguments. First: theology, per Augustine (De Trinitate XIII), is partly wisdom and partly science. If it were only about something not formally eternal, it would be science of it and in no way wisdom, neither by its first subject nor by attribution, since eternal things are not attributed to temporal ones.
claims: Theology is partly wisdom, which concerns eternal things.
If its subject were temporal, it could not be wisdom.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1191.summary: Second persuasion: the higher portion of reason has a proper perfection; if theology's first subject were not eternal (eternal things not being attributed to non-eternal ones), it would in no way concern eternal things and so not perfect the higher portion of reason, and some other habit would be nobler than theology, which is unfitting.
claims: Theology must perfect the higher portion of reason, which concerns eternal things.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1230.summary: Third persuasion: according to Augustine (De Trinitate XIV), this science concerns that by which faith is begotten, defended and strengthened, so it has the same first subject as faith, and faith concerns the first truth.
claims: Theology and faith share the same first subject.
Faith's object is the first truth, God.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1258.summary: Fourth persuasion: the noblest science concerns the noblest genus (Metaphysics VI, De anima I); theology is granted to be the noblest, so it must be about God as subject.
claims: The noblest science concerns the noblest object, God.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1278.summary: Answer to the second (lateral) question, introduced by an example: man can be understood as rational animal (proper quidditative ratio), as substance (in common), as naturally tame (through a proper attribute), or as the noblest animal (in relation to another). The most perfect knowledge cannot be relational (presupposing absolute knowledge), nor through an attribute (presupposing the subject), nor in common (which is confused); so it is quidditative. Likewise a science of God could be posited under a relation ad extra (restorer, governor, head of the Church), under an attribute (e.g. the good), or under a common ratio (being, infinite being, necessary being).
claims: The most perfect knowledge of a thing is through its proper quidditative ratio.
Relational, attributive and common knowledge are less perfect.
Rival views take God as theology's subject under a relation, an attribute, or a common concept.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1362.summary: Against taking God under a common concept: no common concept of God virtually contains the properly theological truths about the plurality of persons. If it did, since we form such concepts naturally, we could naturally understand the immediate propositions about them and from them know the conclusions, acquiring all theology naturally.
claims: No common concept of God virtually contains truths about the Trinity.
Otherwise theology could be acquired naturally.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1411.summary: Second argument against the common-concept view: common concepts are not naturally known to God alone, so neither are the truths included in them; if theology were about God under such a concept, it would not be naturally known to God alone, contrary to what was shown in the first question.
claims: Truths included in common concepts are not naturally known only to God.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1435.summary: Against taking God under an attribute: the same arguments apply, plus special ones. First, knowledge of the quiddity is most perfect (Metaphysics VII), so knowledge of the divine essence is more perfect than knowledge of an attribute, which is like a property of that nature (John Damascene).
claims: Knowledge of essence is more perfect than knowledge of an attribute.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1472.summary: Second: if the attributes differed really from the essence, the essence would be their real cause; so as they differ in ratio, the essence by its ratio has the character of uncaused, while the attributes, though uncaused by identity with the essence, do not by their formal ratio first include being uncaused.
claims: The essence by its own ratio is uncaused; attributes are uncaused only through identity with the essence.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1501.summary: Third: what by its proper ratio more strongly excludes being communicable to many ad extra seems more actual in itself. Such incommunicability belongs to the essence, and to an attribute only as it is of or identical with the infinite essence. If one replies that each attribute is infinite and so incommunicable, their infinity comes from identity with the essence, the root of all intrinsic perfection.
claims: The essence is primarily incommunicable ad extra; attributes are so only through it.
The attributes' infinity derives from the essence.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1545.summary: Against taking God under a relation ad extra: besides the earlier arguments, such relations are relations of reason, and a science not considering its subject under a real ratio is not a real science, as logic is not though it treats things insofar as second intentions apply to them. So theology would not be real.
claims: God's relations to creatures are relations of reason.
A science treating its subject under a ratio of reason is not a real science.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1576.summary: Second: the absolute and the relative do not form one per se concept, so a concept combining them is one only per accidens. No first science is of something one per accidens, since such a science presupposes sciences of each part; so another science about a per se unified concept would be prior.
claims: Absolute and relative make only a per accidens unity.
No first science has a per accidens unity as subject.
concepts: per se and per accidens unity

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1614.summary: Third: no relation ad extra belongs to God necessarily, so nothing theological would belong necessarily to God as theology's subject, and there would be no necessary theological truth. This is also proved by the first and second reasons given for the first question.
claims: Relations ad extra are not necessary to God.
Taking God under such a relation would eliminate necessary theological truths.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1662.summary: Scotus concedes the fourth option: theology is about God under the ratio by which he is this essence (ut haec essentia), as the most perfect science of man would be of man as man, not under a universal or accidental ratio.
claims: Theology in itself is about God as this essence, not under a common, attributive or relational ratio.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1686.summary: On our theology: when a habit has evidence from its object, its first object both virtually contains the habit and, as known, contains its evidence in that intellect. A habit lacking evidence from its object need not have a first object meeting either condition, any more than contingents do; it has as first subject that which is first known, i.e. most perfectly and immediately, through which its first truths are known. Our theology, even of necessary truths, lacks evidence from its object. So its first subject is the first known: infinite being, the most perfect concept we can have of what in itself is the first subject. It meets neither condition, but since our theology of necessary truths concerns the same truths as theology in itself, its first subject is the same as that of theology in itself, though not evident to us.
claims: A habit without evidence from its object need not have a first object that virtually contains or makes evident its truths.
Our theology lacks evidence from its object.
Infinite being is the most perfect concept we can have of theology's subject.
Our theology's first subject is the same as that of theology in itself, though not evident to us.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1828.summary: If one objects that then it is not the first object of our habit, Scotus agrees that it is not the first subject giving evidence, but it is the first subject containing all the truths and apt to give evidence if it were known. This concludes the two questions concerning theology of necessary truths.
claims: The subject of our theology contains all its truths and would give evidence if known.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1857.summary: Turning to contingent theological truths: no subject virtually contains contingent truths about itself, since of itself it is equally open to them and their opposites. But contingent truths have an order, with some first contingent truth; so the first subject of many contingent truths can be posited as that of which the predicate of the first contingent truth (a kind of first principle in the order of contingents) is said first and immediately.
claims: No subject virtually contains contingent truths about it.
Contingent truths are ordered and have a first contingent truth.
The first subject of contingent truths is that of which the first contingent predicate is immediately said.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1906.summary: The first subject of the first contingent truth is that which, seen as such, is first apt to be seen joined to its predicate; for the first known among contingents comes only through intuition of the terms. So the first intuitable thing in which the first predicate of the first contingent truth inheres is the first subject of all ordered contingent truths.
claims: First contingent truths are known only through intuition of their terms.
The first intuitable subject of the first contingent predicate is the first subject of all ordered contingent truths.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1937.summary: So the divine essence, taken as before, is the first subject of contingent theology too, both in itself and as it is in the divine and blessed intellects. The first subject of all theology in itself, of God and the blessed, is the divine essence as this. The blessed's vision of it is like knowledge of being in metaphysics, so the beatific vision is not itself theology but a quasi-perfect simple apprehension of the subject, naturally preceding the science of theology.
claims: The divine essence as this is the first subject of all theology in itself, necessary and contingent.
The beatific vision is not theology but the simple apprehension of its subject, prior to theological science.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e1981.summary: The subject of our contingent theology seems to be the same as that of our necessary theology, in the sense explained: not as virtually containing the habit, even if seen intuitively, but as the knowable closest to us to that in which, intuitively known, the predicate of the first contingent truth would be evidently seen to inhere.
claims: Our contingent theology has the same subject as our necessary theology, as the nearest knowable to the intuitable first subject.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2007.summary: Objection: the Word seems to be the adequate subject of contingent theology, both in itself and in the divine intellect, since it is the first subject of all the articles concerning our restoration.
claims: The Word is the first subject of the articles of redemption.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2025.summary: Reply: some contingent truths are said first of the Word, some of the Holy Spirit, some of the triune God (such as creating). The persons are thus quasi-parts of the subject, as some necessary truths are first true of different persons.
claims: Different contingent truths are said first of different persons or of the Trinity.
The persons are quasi-parts of theology's subject.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2054.summary: Refutation of the view that Christ is theology's first subject: then necessary truths about the Father and Spirit (the Father generates, the Spirit proceeds), contingent truths about them (the Father creates through the Son, the Spirit is sent), and truths about the triune God (omnipotence, immensity, creating, governing, forgiving, punishing, rewarding) would not be theological. A truth belongs per se to a science only if about its first subject, a subjective, integral or essential part, or something essentially attributed to it; but neither the Father, Spirit nor Trinity is Christ, a part of Christ, or essentially attributed to Christ. And since Christ includes a created nature, as subject he would be essentially prior to the Father, which is absurd; nor does his divinity have such priority.
claims: If Christ were the first subject, truths about the Father, Spirit and Trinity would not be theological.
A truth belongs to a science only if about its subject, a part of it, or something attributed to it.
The Father and Trinity cannot be attributed to Christ as essentially prior.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2151.summary: Further arguments against the Christ view: the last two arguments against the relational view (per accidens unity, contingency) apply. So does the first reason of the first question, since necessary truths about the Father, Spirit and Trinity cannot be virtually contained in Christ, as they would hold even had the Word not become incarnate. The third reason also applies: theology would give knowledge of God only as included in Christ, i.e. of the Word only, so not the most distinct knowledge of God, and a prior science would be needed.
claims: Necessary Trinitarian truths would hold even without the Incarnation, so are not virtually contained in Christ.
A Christ-centred theology would not give the most distinct knowledge of God.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2201.summary: Persuasions also support this: Christ's unity as one supposit in two natures is not eternal, yet the first subject's formal unity must be eternal. The argument from faith applies too: 'this man was crucified' is not a theological truth unless the Word is implied in the subject, since the Jews could see the man on the cross naturally; the theological truths are that the Word is a man born of the Virgin, crucified, risen. Articles about the divinity belong first not to Christ as Christ but to other persons or the Trinity. So the adequate object is not Christ but something quasi-common to the Word, the Father and the Spirit.
claims: Christ's hypostatic unity is not eternal, so cannot be the formal unity of theology's first subject.
Theological truths about Christ's humanity have the Word as subject.
The adequate object of theology is something common to the three persons.
concepts: Word as subject of Christological truths

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2282.summary: An analogy from medicine: if the human body is medicine's first subject, with health and sickness as its attributes, and bodies come in kinds (sanguine, phlegmatic), then 'healthy sanguine body' would not be the first subject, both because it is too particular and because it includes an attribute to be considered of the subject, which cannot be the ratio of the subject, since the subject is naturally prior to its attribute.
claims: A first subject cannot be too particular or include an attribute to be demonstrated of it.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2324.summary: In short, whatever is said of some given medical teaching as about such a particular, a per accidens being, the first science of the human body could not be about the healthy sanguine body. Prior sciences could exist, of the human body in common, which has properties known through its common ratio, or of the sanguine body, whose ratio is prior to the healthy sanguine body and virtually contains some of its properties.
claims: A science of a composite particular presupposes prior sciences of its more common components.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2372.summary: Applied: 'Christ' means the Word as man (Damascene). Before knowledge of Christ as first subject, there would naturally be prior knowledge of the Word (of what belongs to it as Word) and, before that, of God (of what belongs to God as common to the three persons).
claims: Knowledge of God as common to three persons is prior to knowledge of the Word, which is prior to knowledge of Christ.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2402.summary: So if theology in itself is first knowledge, it is not first of Christ; and since it concerns truths common and proper to the three persons equally, its adequate subject is not any one person but God as common to the three. Then every theological truth is about the first subject (what belongs to God as God), about a quasi-subjective part (what is proper to a person), or about something attributed to the subject or a part (creatures in their relation to God, and the assumed nature in its relation to the sustaining Word).
claims: Theology's adequate subject is God as common to the three persons.
Every theological truth concerns the subject, a quasi-subjective part (a person), or something attributed to them.
concepts: God as common to three persons

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2463.summary: Another view, Grosseteste's in his Hexaemeron: Christ is first subject as one in a threefold unity (with the Father and Spirit, of the Word with the assumed nature, and of head with members). In its favour: God as subject does not contain the seven articles about the humanity, since they do not belong to God by the divine nature; a subject first contains an attribute through whose form the attribute inheres. Christ contains these, since they belong to him by humanity, and also really contains the articles of the Deity, which belong to him by divinity.
claims: Christ is one by a threefold unity (Grosseteste).
God as such does not contain the articles about Christ's humanity, while Christ contains both sets.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2528.summary: Second argument for that view: the subjects of the parts of a doctrine must fall under the subject of the whole as subjective or quasi-integral parts, but the subjects of parts of Scripture do not fall under God thus. Glosses at the start of books assign material causes that are not anything of God; e.g. the gloss on Hosea says its matter is the ten tribes.
claims: Subjects of parts of a doctrine must fall under the subject of the whole.
Glosses assign scriptural books subjects that are not anything of God.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2561.summary: Third argument: some books of Scripture narrate nothing proper about God, since they recount no deed requiring more on God's part than general influence; so such a book is not about God.
claims: Some scriptural books narrate only events involving God's general influence.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2579.summary: Reply to the first argument: contingent truths about Christ are virtually contained in no subject as an attribute is in its subject, or they would be necessary. Yet they have a subject of which they are said immediately and first, the Word: the theological truths of Incarnation, Passion, Nativity are 'the Word became man', 'the Word is a man born', 'the Word is a man who suffered'.
claims: Contingent truths about Christ are not virtually contained in any subject.
Their immediate subject is the Word.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2613.summary: To the claim that these attributes inhere by reason of the humanity: humanity is not the ratio of the first subject at which resolution stops but a quasi-prior attribute mediating between the first subject of these truths, the Word, and later attributes such as being born. Humanity cannot be the ratio of the subject for the first attribute, being incarnate, which is said of the Word without presupposing humanity in it as in a subject.
claims: Humanity is a quasi-attribute mediating between the Word and later Christological predicates.
Being incarnate is said of the Word without presupposing humanity in it.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2646.summary: Reply to the second argument: it suffices that partial subjects be attributed to the first subject, and the matter the glosses assign to each book can be so attributed to God. Alternatively, each book's matter is God, of whom it narrates how he governed humanity, while the people or person governed is remote matter; this is how such glosses are to be understood.
claims: Partial subjects need only be attributed to the first subject.
Each scriptural book's proper matter is God as governing humanity; the people governed are remote matter.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2685.summary: Reply to the third argument: even a book with no miracle contains God's providence and governance of humanity or a people or person. If Moses in Exodus and an Egyptian chronicler wrote the same history of Pharaoh, Moses' subject would be God, governing by mercifully freeing the oppressed Jews, justly punishing the Egyptians, wisely ordering their liberation so the people would gladly receive the law, and powerfully working signs; the chronicler's subject would be the Egyptian kingdom, king or people. For the chronicler God's acts are incidental; for Moses they are principal and the matter is incidental.
claims: Every scriptural book concerns God's providence and governance.
The same events can belong to different sciences depending on what is principal and what incidental.
Scripture's history has God as subject; secular history has human agents as subject.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2759.summary: Even where no miracle is narrated, what God permitted, assisting by common influence and not preventing, is what the book principally intends as part of Scripture. How it was ordered to others' good, or justly punished if evil, is often added in the same or another book; and if permitted and unpunished, Scripture elsewhere says in general it will be punished.
claims: Scripture principally concerns what God does or permits, even through common influence.
Scripture shows how permitted evils are ordered to good or punished.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2803.summary: Replies to the first two arguments of the main question. Boethius speaks of the subject of accidents, not the subject of consideration. On Physics II, Aristotle means matter 'out of which', not 'in which' or 'about which'. Better: a science's subject belongs to efficient, not material, causality; it is called 'matter' by likeness to making, where object-about-which and receptive matter coincide because making is transitive. The act of science is not received in its object but remains in the knower; it 'passes' only in that it terminates in something about which it is, and for this feature the subject is called matter.
claims: Boethius' dictum concerns the subject of accidents, not of a science.
A science's subject is properly an efficient cause of the science, called matter only by analogy.
The act of knowing remains in the knower though it is about its object.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2873.summary: Reply to the argument from Posterior Analytics I: the subject of any naturally discovered science is a universal and so has subjective parts. But this science's subject is this essence as singular, since being divided among many singulars is an imperfection of created universal natures; removing that imperfection, the divine essence is knowable without division into subjective parts. Still, the divine persons can be called quasi-subjective parts of the essence, though the essence is not numbered in them.
claims: Natural sciences have universal subjects with subjective parts; theology's subject is a singular essence.
Division into singulars is an imperfection of created natures.
The divine persons are quasi-subjective parts of the essence, which is not multiplied in them.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2926.summary: On attributes: some say the divine attributes are quasi-properties of the essence, but this fails, since considering attributes we can naturally understand belongs to metaphysics, unless there are attributes belonging per se to this essence as this and not as now naturally and confusedly understood. That a property lies outside its subject's essence is true where the property is really caused by the subject; in God what has the character of a property is uncaused, passing into the essence by identity, yet as to knowability it is known through the essence's ratio as if really distinct.
claims: Naturally knowable divine attributes belong to metaphysics.
In God properties are not caused by the subject but identical with it, though known through it as if distinct.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e2976.summary: On principles: the principles of a knowable subject need not be principles of the subject in itself; being as being, the subject of metaphysics, has no principles, else they would be principles of every being. Rather, every subject must have principles through which its properties are demonstrated of it, from which, as middle terms, complex principles such as self-evident propositions are formed. In this way any subject, however unprincipled in itself, has principles relative to its properties.
claims: A science's principles need not be causes of its subject.
Any subject has principles as middles for demonstrating its properties.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3022.summary: Heading introducing replies to the arguments of the second way (that something other than God is the subject).

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3032.summary: Reply to Augustine's things-and-signs division: it states the matter of this science in general, not its formal first subject.
claims: Things and signs are theology's matter in general, not its formal subject.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3045.summary: Reply to the four senses: any sense that is not literal in one part of Scripture is literal in another, so although parts of Scripture have several senses, Scripture as a whole has all of them as literal sense; so there are not four subjects.
claims: Every spiritual sense in one passage is the literal sense elsewhere in Scripture.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3065.summary: Reply to the third argument (man as subject): it argues for the opposite, in two ways. First, man is subject of moral science or medicine because he virtually contains all their truths: the human body contains the ratio of health given its complexion, and the soul contains the ratio of natural happiness (Ethics I). But man does not contain the ratio of this science's end, since a supernatural end or object is not included in the ratio of man; so he cannot be its first subject.
claims: Man is the subject of medicine and ethics because he virtually contains their truths.
The supernatural end is not contained in the ratio of man, so man is not theology's subject.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3117.summary: Second: man is the ultimate end of those sciences, to which health and natural happiness are ordered, since all love of concupiscence presupposes love of friendship. Health and happiness are loved with concupiscence, so what is loved with friendship, man (body and soul), is a further end. So if man were theology's subject by body or soul, the end would be the subject of the science.
claims: Love of concupiscence presupposes love of friendship.
Man, loved with love of friendship, is the further end to which health and happiness are ordered.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3163.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: its first premiss is false. A science's end is nothing but to attain its proper object by its act, not to induce a form in the object, since science is not productive.
claims: The end of a science is to attain its object by its act, not to produce a form in it.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3188.summary: Reply to Hugh and Cassiodorus in the second question: they speak not of the formal subject but of the proximate matter, which Scripture treats more extensively because of its more immediate ordering to the end.
claims: The works of restoration and the whole Christ are proximate matter, not formal subject, of theology.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3211.summary: Reply to the argument from metaphysics: metaphysics is not about God as first subject. Beyond the special sciences there must be a common science proving in common what is common to them; so there must be a common science of being, treating the properties of being presupposed in the special sciences. If there were a natural science of God besides, there would still be another of being as being.
claims: Metaphysics is not about God as first subject.
A common science of being as being is required besides the special sciences.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3257.summary: On Metaphysics VI: Aristotle's argument concludes only that the noblest science concerns the noblest genus either as first object or as considered in that science in the most perfect way possible in a naturally acquired science. God, though not metaphysics' first subject, is considered there in the noblest way possible for natural science.
claims: Metaphysics treats God in the noblest way possible for natural science, without God being its first subject.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3301.summary: On Averroes' criticism of Avicenna: Avicenna was right and Averroes wrong. First, if the existence of separate substances were presupposed in metaphysics and proved in natural philosophy, natural philosophy would be simply prior to all metaphysics, since it would establish whether metaphysics' subject exists.
claims: Avicenna, not Averroes, is right that metaphysics proves the first cause exists.
Otherwise physics would be prior to metaphysics.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3340.summary: Second: any condition of an effect that cannot belong to it without its cause can demonstrate quia that the cause exists. Metaphysics considers many properties (multiplicity, dependence, composition) that cannot exist without a first cause, which show something actually simple, independent and necessary. The first cause is shown more perfectly from metaphysical properties than from natural ones like motion, since knowing it as first being or necessary being is more perfect and immediate than knowing it as first mover.
claims: Metaphysical properties of beings demonstrate the existence of a first cause.
The metaphysical route to God is more perfect than the physical route via the first mover.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3402.summary: Reply to the argument from end and goodness: the ratio of end is not the noblest ratio of cognition; rather what is the end, as foundation of that relation, is. Deity is the fundamental ratio of God's being end to creatures, so God is first object, which supports Scotus. Even if goodness is by appropriation the foundation of end, deity is its root. It does follow that if there is no ultimate end there is no good, since what is ordered to something else has diminished goodness; but goodness is not the proper ratio of end, the essence is. Avicenna should be read as about the foundation of the end.
claims: The noblest ratio is the foundation of being end, the deity, not the ratio of end itself.
Without an ultimate end nothing would be perfectly good.
The divine essence, not goodness, is the fundamental ratio of God as end.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3485.summary: On the third (lateral) question, a probable first answer: theology is not about everything knowable, since quiddities distinct from the divine essence first contain many truths about themselves; even if, per impossibile, they were uncreated and all else removed, they would contain them, as line and number contain their immediate propositions. On this view there would be distinct scientific habits in the divine intellect: theology caused by the divine essence, geometry by virtue of line, arithmetic by virtue of number.
claims: Created quiddities first contain truths about themselves.
On this view God would have distinct sciences caused by distinct objects.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3545.summary: Against that view, first: the divine intellect would be debased by being acted on by something other than its essence. In the instant it understands the line, it would be as if in potency to truths in the line and know them by its virtue, so the line would quasi-effectively impress knowledge in the divine intellect and move it.
claims: The divine intellect cannot be moved by created objects without being debased.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3582.summary: Second: any power actuated per se by diverse objects through their own virtue has as first object something common to them. If the line caused truth in the divine intellect, so would other things, and the divine intellect's first object would be something common, not the singular divine essence. Attribution of the other objects to the essence would not help, as other beings are attributed to substance yet our intellect's object is being.
claims: A power moved by diverse objects by their own virtue has a common first object.
Then the divine essence would not be the first object of God's intellect.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3621.summary: Third: if the divine essence is the first object, it is so not by community of predication but by virtue; and it would not be first object by virtue if anything else moved the divine intellect by its own virtue.
claims: The divine essence is first object of God's intellect by virtue, not by predication.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3644.summary: Scotus's own answer: God's theology is about all knowables, since its first object makes everything else actually known in his intellect. In the first sign (instant) of nature the divine essence is known; in the second, quiddities that virtually contain their truths; in the third, those truths. The order of second to third is not causal, as if the quiddities caused anything in his intellect, but an order of effects essentially ordered to one cause. Example: if the sun lit a near part and a far opaque part illuminable only by the sun, there would be an order between them, but not of cause to effect.
claims: God's theology covers all knowables because the divine essence makes them all known.
There is an order of instants of nature in divine knowledge: essence, quiddities, truths.
Created quiddities do not cause anything in the divine intellect; they are ordered effects of the same cause.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3733.summary: Applied: the divine essence makes other quiddities actually known in God's intellect and, as if posterior by nature, makes the truths they contain known. Finite quiddities have no power to move the divine intellect, since the infinite is in no way perfected by the finite; if the divine nature did not move it to further knowledge in the third instant, the divine intellect would never know those truths, having no other mover.
claims: Finite quiddities cannot move or perfect the infinite divine intellect.
The divine essence alone moves God's intellect to know all truths.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3779.summary: So God has only theological knowledge of all knowables, since it is all by virtue of the first theological object. God's theology is not only about all things but is all knowledge God can have of them, and absolutely it is, for anything, all knowledge that includes no imperfection, since it alone is not limited; any other knowledge, coming from a limited cause, is limited.
claims: All of God's knowledge is theological.
God's theology is all unlimited knowledge of anything knowable.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3825.summary: The created intellects of the blessed are different: they can be moved by created quiddities to know their truths, so besides theological knowledge of them as shown in God's essence, they can have natural knowledge from the quiddities' own motion. So the theology of the blessed is not all the knowledge of creatures possible to them.
claims: The blessed can have natural knowledge of creatures besides theological knowledge.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3862.summary: Whether theology is about all things even if other sciences treat some: distinguish theology in itself from theology as a habit perfecting a blessed intellect. In itself it covers all knowables, since all can be known by virtue of its first object. As in the blessed, it can cover any and even all knowables, these being finite, but in fact it is limited by God's will in what he shows in his essence, so it extends to as much as he voluntarily shows them.
claims: Theology in itself is about all knowables.
The theology of the blessed extends as far as God wills to show them in his essence.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3910.summary: Our theology is not actually of all knowables in this state, since, like that of the blessed, it is limited by the will of God revealing. The limit set by the divine will for general revelation is what is in Scripture (Revelation 22: whoever adds to these things). So our theology in fact concerns only what is contained in Scripture and what can be drawn from it.
claims: Our theology is limited by God's revealing will.
For general revelation the limit is Scripture and what can be derived from it.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3949.summary: Nor could our theology possibly be of everything: our intellect cannot conceive many quiddities specifically, and revelation by common law concerns only things whose terms we can naturally conceive; and, according to some, our revealed theology cannot coexist with evident knowledge of the same knowables, so it cannot extend to what we know naturally.
claims: Revelation by common law concerns only things whose terms we can naturally conceive.
According to some, revealed theology cannot coexist with evident knowledge of the same matters.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e3995.summary: Yet all theology, ours, the blessed's, or God's, is about all beings as to some of what is knowable of them, namely their relations to the divine essence as this essence. A relation cannot be known without both terms, so a relation to this essence as this cannot be known without knowing this essence as this.
claims: All theology concerns all beings in their relations to the divine essence as this.
Knowledge of such relations requires knowledge of the divine essence as this.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e4026.summary: So, truly speaking, theology is about everything and is all knowledge that includes no imperfection; in God's intellect, which can have no imperfect knowledge, it is all knowledge. It is not all knowledge simply for created intellects, since they can have other knowledge from a special quiddity moving them. It alone is knowledge of all things as to their relation to this essence as this, provided the essence as this, not as some naturally intelligible attribute, terminates the creature's relation.
claims: Theology is about everything and is all knowledge free of imperfection.
For created intellects theology is not all knowledge, but it alone knows all things in their relation to God as this essence.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e4072.summary: This is perhaps one reason why we cannot know that the created intellect is ordered to this end as this: we cannot know the relation founded in intellectual nature to this essence as its proper end, since we do not know the term of the relation; nor, therefore, the image in that nature as the saints speak of it.
claims: We cannot naturally know our ordering to God as this essence, since we do not know the term of the relation.
Hence the image of God in us is not naturally knowable in the saints' sense.

jdso8u-d1e110-d1e4103.summary: Reply to the first argument of the third question: Augustine's denial concerns theology not in itself but as handed down in Sacred Scripture.
claims: Augustine's restriction applies to theology as contained in Scripture, not theology in itself.

jdso8u-d1e110.summary: Ordinatio I, Prologue part 3, three questions combined (Wadding q.3 and lateral qq.1-2): whether theology is about God as first subject, whether under some special ratio, and whether about all things by attribution to that subject. Scotus distinguishes theology in itself (what its object can cause in a proportioned intellect) from theology in us, defines the first subject as what first and virtually contains all the truths of a habit (against taking it as merely the most common object), and divides theology into necessary truths (God ad intra) and contingent ones (God ad extra). Theology in itself has God as first subject, under the ratio of this essence (ut haec), not under a common concept such as infinite being, an attribute such as goodness, or a relation ad extra such as restorer or head of the Church; Christ (against a Christocentric view and Grosseteste's threefold unity) and man are rejected as first subjects, contingent Christological truths having the Word as immediate subject. For our theology, which lacks evidence from its object, the first known subject is infinite being, our most perfect concept of the same essence. The beatific vision is the simple apprehension of theology's subject, not theology itself. Along the way Scotus argues that metaphysics is about being, not God, and sides with Avicenna against Averroes on proving God's existence in metaphysics. On scope: God's theology is all his knowledge, created quiddities never moving the divine intellect (instants of nature); the blessed's theology extends as far as God wills to show; ours is limited to Scripture and what follows from it, yet all theology concerns all things in their relation to God as this essence.
claims: The first subject of a science is what first and virtually contains all its truths.
The first subject of theology in itself is God as this essence.
The first subject of our theology is the divine essence, conceived by us at best as infinite being.
Neither Christ nor man is theology's first subject.
Metaphysics is about being as being, and can prove the existence of a first cause.
All of God's knowledge is theological; created quiddities do not move the divine intellect.
Our theology is in fact limited to what is in Scripture and derivable from it.
concepts: theology in itself and in us
